stem: A 16-year-old boy has new involuntary jerky movements, depression and falling school grades. His father has the same illness, which has passed from parent to child in every generation of the family. His father's sister did not become ill until her 60s.
oneliner: 16M + jerky movements, depression, falling grades; affected father, dominant in every generation, aunt ill only in her 60s → why so early?
ask: Which mechanism best explains this boy's early onset?

options.A: Differential imprinting of the maternal and paternal alleles
options.B: Mitochondrial DNA variants passed on only by the mother
options.C: Rescue by modifier genes that differ between relatives
options.D: Expansion of an unstable repeat on passage to the child
options.E: A single codon change altering one amino acid

whyNot.A: **Imprinting** silences one parent's allele in every carrier; it does not make onset **decades earlier** in the next generation
whyNot.B: **Mitochondrial** DNA passes only through the mother, but here an **affected father** transmits it
whyNot.C: **Modifier genes** would not give a **teen onset** in the son of an **affected father** against a **60s onset** in his aunt
whyNot.E: A **single codon change** is stable between generations, so it would not bring onset forward from the **60s to the teens**

answer: Trinucleotide (CAG) repeat expansion with anticipation (Huntington disease)
why: Chorea, depression and cognitive decline in a **dominant** family is **Huntington disease**, a CAG repeat disorder. The repeat **lengthens on transmission, most through spermatogenesis**, so onset comes earlier and is more severe (**anticipation**); juvenile cases usually inherit from the **father**.

idea.rule: Unstable trinucleotide repeats expand on transmission, so later generations fall ill earlier (anticipation).
also: Huntington repeats expand most through the father
Fragile X (CGG) expands to a full mutation in maternal transmission
Myotonic dystrophy (CTG) shows anticipation, with a congenital form from affected mothers
Friedreich ataxia is a GAA repeat inherited recessively

stem: A 30-year-old man falls asleep several times a day at work despite a full night in bed. He sees vivid images as he drifts off, cannot move for about a minute on waking, and his knees buckle when he laughs hard. Examination is normal.
oneliner: 30M + daily sleep attacks, vivid images falling asleep, paralysis on waking, knees buckle with laughter, normal exam → which HLA allele?
ask: Which HLA allele is most strongly associated with this condition?

whyNot.B: **HLA-B27** goes with spondyloarthritis; his picture is a **sleep-wake disorder** with cataplexy
whyNot.C: **HLA-DQ2/DQ8** go with celiac disease and type 1 diabetes, not with **sleep attacks and cataplexy**
whyNot.D: **HLA-B51** goes with Behcet disease, not with **sleep attacks, sleep paralysis and cataplexy**
whyNot.E: **HLA-DR4** goes with rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes, not with a **sleep-wake disorder**

why: Sleep attacks, **hypnagogic hallucinations**, **sleep paralysis** and **cataplexy** (knees buckling with laughter) make **narcolepsy type 1**, with loss of hypocretin (orexin) neurons. It is strongly linked to **HLA-DQB1*06:02**.

idea.rule: Narcolepsy with cataplexy is tied to HLA-DQB1*06:02 and low CSF hypocretin-1.
also: Loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus causes type 1 narcolepsy
